rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses the same vivid personifying mode as poetic images of a corner kissing a footprint and a minbar walking toward its addressee; Hell is shown speaking, seeing, and nearly bursting with rage.
rows.anchor: يوم نقول لجهنم هل امتلأت وتقول هل من مزيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqillani calls mumathalah, which Qudama names tamthil, a metaphorical figure opposite irdaf: it compresses an allusion by choosing words that themselves exemplify the intended meaning; this verse is an example.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا الباب في القرآن قوله

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asma'i reads thiyab, literally clothes, as the body; Arabic also uses expressions such as my two garments be your ransom to mean oneself.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي أراد البدن قال

rows.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد والأصمعي وعبد الله بن المعتز
rows.claim: Most authorities define mutabaqa as mentioning a thing together with its opposite, such as night and day or black and white; al-Khalil, al-Asma'i, and Ibn al-Mu'tazz hold this account.
rows.anchor: ويرون من البديع أيضا ما يسمونه المطابقة وأكثرهم على أن معناها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet recalled seeing Quss ibn Sa'ida at Ukaz atop a red camel, preaching that people should gather, listen, understand, and speak truthfully, since all living things die.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال لما وفد وفد عبد القيس على رسول الله قال أيكم يعرف قس بن ساعدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: At the Prophet's request, the delegation recited Quss's verses: generations leave signs, death has no return, and all people ultimately go where the dead have gone.
rows.anchor: ثم قال رسول الله أيكم يروي شعره فأنشدوه

rows.speaker: هشام عن أبيه
rows.claim: Hisham, reporting from his father, says an Iyad delegation told the Prophet of Quss's verses about the dead in their graves being summoned on a coming Day, some naked and some in worn clothing.
rows.anchor: عن هشام عن أبيه أن وفدا من إياد قدموا على رسول الله فسألهم عن حال قس بن ساعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech can depict inner thought and feeling through gesture, indication, or explicit eloquent wording; verbal expression and signs each have different degrees and levels.
rows.anchor: وتصوير ما في النفس وتشكيل ما في القلب حتى تعلمه وكأنك مشاهده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Description ranges from accurate portrayal to excess or shortfall, and varies in precision, beauty, brevity, explanation, completeness, and approximation.
rows.anchor: ورب وصف يصور لك الموصوف كما هو على جهته لا خلف فيه ورب وصف ببر عليه ويتعداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He contrasts concise portrayal, as in the sleepers' fear, with extended exposition of the Resurrection's terrors; the detailed scenes make that Day vivid.
rows.anchor: وهذا مما يصور الشيء على جهته ويمثل أهوال ذلك اليوم

words: وَمَا تَنقِمُ مِنَّآ إِلَّآ أَنْ ءَامَنَّا بِـَٔايَٰتِ رَبِّنَا لَمَّا جَآءَتْنَا
رَبَّنَآ أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًۭا وَتَوَفَّنَا مُسْلِمِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sorcerers' answer to Pharaoh's threat is an instance of speech rendered within a scene; Baqillani links it to their parallel declaration that they return to God and hope for forgiveness.
rows.anchor: إنا إلى ربنا منقلبون وما تنقم منا إلا أن آمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had the opponents been able to answer the challenge, they would have weakened the Prophet's claim and scattered his followers; their failure despite ample time proves they could not match or undermine the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: فلما لم يفعلوا شيئا من ذلك مع طول المدة ووقوع الفسحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an describes its opponents as contentious, supporting the claim that their silence was inability rather than lack of argumentative skill.
rows.anchor: وقد أخبر الله تعالى عنهم أنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their shifting claims that the Qur'an was imitable, ancient tales, forged magic, poetry, madness, fabrication, or sorcery show confusion and excuse-making in place of a successful counter-text.
rows.anchor: إلى آيات كثيرة في نحو هذا تدل على أنهم كانوا متحيرين في أمرهم متعجبين من عجزهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They waged war, severed kinship, risked their lives, and demanded signs and angels, all in an effort to defeat him by some means.
rows.anchor: وقد علم منهم أنهم ناصبوه الحرب وجاهدوه ونابذوه وقطعوا الأرحام وأخطروا بأنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Buhturi calls such polished lines veins of gold and shows technical mastery, yet Baqillani finds their ornament can conceal weaknesses in imagery and meaning.
rows.anchor: وكان البحتري يسمي نحو هذه الأبيات عروق الذهب وفي نحوه ما يدل على براعته في الصناعة وحذقه في البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lightning-like khayal imagery is overworked: linking its light to the subterranean depths of Batn Wajrah is a flaw, since faint light does not affect what lies below ground.
rows.anchor: وهذا غلو في الصنعة إلا أن ذكره بطن وجره حشو وفي ذكره خلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming several landmarks to locate the scene is padding; Baqillani compares it to Imru al-Qays giving four boundaries as if he feared a property sale would fail for want of a boundary.
rows.anchor: وتحديده المكان - على الحشو - أحمد من تحديد امرئ القيس من ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects reading the line as a new flash of lightning from the beloved's direction: that break damages the praised poetic order, and the image adds no useful information.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يقدر مقدر أن البحتري قطع الكلام الأول وابتدأ بذكر برق لمع من ناحية حبيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quoted pilgrimage stanza has artful openings and endings and sweet wording, but little semantic content or benefit.
rows.anchor: هذه ألفاظ بديعة المطالع والمقاطع حلوة المجاني والمواقع قليلة المعاني والفوائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates prose badi' with Ali's balanced saying that patience and forbearance are twins born of high aspiration; aphorisms on a person's worth and knowledge's key, Khalid ibn al-Walid's wordplay, Hajjaj's trust, and Bedouin sayings add examples.
rows.anchor: هما توأمان ينتجهما علو الهمة وقال قيمة كل امرئ ما يحسن وقال العلم قفل ومفتاحه المسئلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalid ibn al-Walid's phrase about breaking the Persians' service plays on khidmah as a circular ring; anklets are called khadam for that same ring shape.
rows.anchor: والخدمة الحلقة المستديرة ولذلك قيل للخلاخيل خدام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imru al-Qays's qaid al-awabid is both badi' and metaphor: a swift horse released after game becomes its fetter by catching it; later poets imitate the phrase in images of eyes, gazes, and speech.
rows.anchor: قوله قيد الأوابد عندهم من البديع ومن الاستعارة ويرونه من الألفاظ الشريقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening line is disconnected from what precedes and offers only familiar paronomasia, so its repeated wordplay is not truly novel.
rows.anchor: فالبيت الأول منقطع عما قبله وليس فيه شئ غير التجنيس الذي ليس ببديع لتكرره على كل لسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about one distance following another is pleasing, but its device is well-worn; the second line is close to its predecessor in wording and meaning, and saying that good is not done unhurriedly is poor diction.
rows.anchor: ما أخذ المدى بعد المدى فإنه لفظ مليح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of pulling stars down with reins is extremely objectionable; the following line is unrelated, opens badly, and uses an unmotivated interrogative turn.
rows.anchor: فالبيت الأول منكر جدا في جر النجوم بالأرسان من موضعه إلى العلو والتكلف فيه واقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two lines are alien to the poem, and the panegyric that follows with a pledge of self-sacrifice and a wish to meet Abu Sa'id does not sound like the poet's style.
rows.anchor: والبيتان أجنبيان من كلامه غريبان في قصيدته ولم يقع له في المدح في هذه القصيدة شئ جيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat naming Mudar, Rabia, and Azd has a good meaning, but place names prevent stylistic refinement; the same idea is expressed better in the line about all people becoming angry when Banu Tamim are.
rows.anchor: البيت الأول حسن المعنى وإن كانت ألفاظه بذكر الأماكن لا يتأتى فيه التحسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next line is poorly joined to what precedes and clumsy in diction; forced rhyme and genealogy spoil the poem.
rows.anchor: والبيت الثاني قد تعذر عليه وصله بما سبق من الكلام على وجه يلطف وهو قبيح اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinas can be formed by adding or dropping a letter, or through near-similar forms; he illustrates the device with lines from al-Buhturi, Ibn Muqbil, Zuhayr, Abu Tammam, Abu Nuwas, Ibn al-Mu'tazz, and al-Mutanabbi.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون التجنيس بزيادة حرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some count Qur'anic wording among this kind of wordplay, including the paired forms in the challenge not to hasten and the contrast between declaring worship of God and telling others to worship as they wish.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن من هذا القبيل قوله عز وجل

words: ثم إذا مسكم الضر فإليه تجأرون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muqabalah coordinates meanings with corresponding or opposing meanings; the cited Qur'anic passage contrasts turning to God in distress with a group's later associating partners after relief.
rows.anchor: ويعدون من البديع المقابلة وهي أن يوفق بين معان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If humans could compose a counterpart, earlier Arabic speeches, letters, sermons, poetry, and saj' would have supplied one; the preserved literary record contains no such precedent, showing the Qur'an has no equal.
rows.anchor: فلما لم نرهم احتجوا عليه بكلام سابق وخطبة متقدمة ورسالة سالفة ونظم بديع ولا عارضوه به

rows.speaker: معترض
rows.claim: An objection says the miracle rests on the public challenge and widely transmitted failure to answer it, so proving incapacity independently would seem to diminish the challenge's role.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل الذي بنى عليه الأمر في تثبيت معجزة القرآن أنه وقع التحدي إلى الإتيان بمثله وأنهم عجزوا عنه بعد التحدي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqillani answers that the challenge establishes proof publicly, removes doubt by making incapacity visible to all, and binds experts in eloquence through the Qur'an itself.
rows.anchor: قيل إنما احتيج إلى التحدي لإقامة الحجة وإظهار وجه البرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance and clarification depend on the favor, completeness, and intellect God grants; the Qur'an is a light by which He guides, while those deprived of divine support cannot find a way out.
rows.anchor: وعلى حسب ما آتى من الفضل وأعطى من الكمال والعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reader who understands should thank God and ask for more knowledge; a doubter should keep studying rhetoric and gain expertise until reaching the sound path.
rows.anchor: فاحمد الله على ما رزقك من الفهم إن فهمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic fluency does not explain rejection: opponents differed as ignorant, stubborn, envious, ungrateful, or poor in reasoning, while poets such as Labid, Ka'b, and Hassan accepted Islam; the first generation itself shone with learning and eloquence.
rows.anchor: ولا يوسوس إليك الشيطان بأنه قد كان ممن هو أعلم منك بالعربية وأدرب منك في الفصاحة أقوام
